objectives.text: The learner can name the three stages in order and say where each happens
The learner can explain why oxygen is needed even though it appears only at the very end
The learner can account for the ATP yield roughly

steps.note: the three stages and where they happen

say: One glucose molecule goes in, and about thirty molecules of usable energy come out. It happens in three stages, in two different places in the cell, and the order matters because each stage hands its output to the next one.

Glycolysis is the oldest part and the simplest, and it happens out in the cytoplasm. It splits the six carbon sugar into two three carbon molecules, and it needs no oxygen at all. Note that it spends two ATP to get started, which is why the net yield is only two.

board.text: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP to make 4. Biology often has to invest before it earns.

say: Now the part that confuses people. Oxygen turns up only in the last stage, so why does the whole thing stop without it? Because the carriers have nowhere to put their electrons, and once every carrier is full, the earlier stages jam.

board.text: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. Without it the chain backs up, NAD+ is never regenerated, and glycolysis stalls too.

say: That is also why fermentation exists. It makes no extra energy at all. Its only job is to hand those electrons somewhere so that glycolysis can keep turning over. Two ATP per glucose instead of thirty, but two is a great deal better than nothing.

board.text: Fermentation regenerates NAD+. That is its whole purpose — it is not an energy source.
About 30 ATP with oxygen, 2 without. A fifteenfold difference.

summary: We placed the three stages in the cell, tracked what each hands to the next, explained why oxygen is load-bearing despite appearing only at the end, and accounted for the ATP tally.
